public_rationale: He forecasts that 'at some point' Anthropic and OpenAI will hold compute reservations they don't need and can't afford because of mistimed growth projections. He sets no deadline. The contract treats the forecast as supported early if a filing or credible report shows OpenAI or Anthropic writing down, cancelling, reselling or defaulting on committed compute because demand fell short and it cannot pay. If only one company meets this, the contract counts it as partial. On 26 October 2026, Fortune reported that Anthropic's S-1 names periods of excess or underutilized compute as a risk. The same report says Anthropic has underestimated its compute needs in the past and been capacity constrained (e1). Fortune also reports $974 million in operating income for Anthropic's second quarter and $112.4 billion in cash as of late June 2026 (e2). On 15 April 2026, CNBC reported that OpenAI dropped plans to rent capacity directly from a Norway data center, days after confirming it paused a UK project (e3). A CNBC source said OpenAI and the Norway operator did not agree an offtake deal. OpenAI said it was in talks to rent that capacity from Microsoft under existing contracted spending (e3). None of these items shows either company writing down, cancelling, reselling or defaulting on committed compute. The forecast remains open.
limitations: Anthropic's position comes from Fortune's summary of the S-1, not from the filing itself.
No OpenAI financial filings or utilization data were read.
The evidence does not give the terms of, or the reason for, the paused UK project.
Secondary reports on OpenAI moving to leased compute were not read.
The evidence covers dates up to late October 2026 and says nothing about later periods.

statement.document_title: The Subprime AI Crisis Is Here

from_speaker: will be left with a bunch of compute reservations
they don't need and can't afford
our_interpretation: Plain reading: each company ends up holding committed compute it cannot use and cannot pay for, because demand grew more slowly than planned.
Signs would include write-downs, cancellation or resale of committed capacity, payment defaults, or the company itself saying it has unneeded capacity it cannot afford.
Dropping talks on a deal that was never signed, or shifting how compute is sourced, does not by itself meet this.
criteria.support_condition: A dated disclosure or credible report that OpenAI or Anthropic holds committed compute that is surplus to demand and that it cannot afford, tied to growth that fell short of plans.
criteria.contradiction_condition: No deadline, so it cannot be contradicted outright. Evidence that both companies remain capacity-constrained and can pay their commitments argues against it for now.

evidence.excerpt: Anthropic also disclosed that it has significantly underestimated its compute requirements in the past, leaving it capacity constrained and impacting product development.
evidence.explanation: Anthropic names excess compute as a risk, but says its actual problem so far has been too little compute, not too much.

evidence.excerpt: Revenue has kept pace with compute expenses, and in its second quarter, the company generated $974 million in operating income. It also held $112.4 billion in cash and cash equivalents as of late June.
evidence.explanation: As of mid-2026, Anthropic was not unable to afford its compute. That does not rule out the forecast later.

evidence.excerpt: OpenAI has abandoned plans to rent compute capacity directly from a Norwegian data center, days after confirming it paused a similar project in the U.K.
evidence.explanation: OpenAI pulled back from planned capacity, but the offtake deal was never signed, and OpenAI said it would rent the compute through Microsoft under existing contracts. This is not unneeded, unaffordable committed compute.

public_payload.what_would_resolve: A filing or credible report that OpenAI or Anthropic wrote down, cancelled, resold or defaulted on committed compute because demand fell short of projections and it could not pay. Under the contract, one company alone would count as partial; both would fully meet the forecast.
